lessons.title: Worked Examples: Comparing Both Regimes Across Salary Levels

children.text: Rules and breakevens become real only when you see them run on actual lives. This lesson walks through five salaried Indians, from a ₹7 lakh first job in Jaipur to a ₹40 lakh role in Mumbai, each with a realistic set of rent, investments and loans. Find the one closest to you and study it closely.

body.text: Every result in this table was predictable before doing a single slab calculation. Compare the benefits column with the breakeven column, and the winner falls out.

children.text: 1. Aman, ₹7 Lakh: The First Job

Aman, 24, is a junior analyst at a Jaipur bank. His basic salary is ₹3,00,000 with HRA of ₹1,20,000. He shares a flat and pays ₹8,000 a month rent. His only 80C item is ₹36,000 of EPF. Rajasthan levies no professional tax.
HRA exemption: least of ₹1,20,000 received, rent ₹96,000 minus 10% of basic ₹30,000 (₹66,000), and 40% of basic (₹1,20,000). Exemption ₹66,000.

Old regime: ₹7,00,000 minus ₹66,000 HRA, ₹50,000 standard deduction and ₹36,000 80C gives taxable income of ₹5,48,000. Tax is ₹12,500 plus 20% of ₹48,000 (₹9,600), total ₹22,100. No rebate above ₹5 lakh. Cess ₹884. Total ₹22,984.
New regime: ₹7,00,000 minus ₹75,000 is ₹6,25,000, below ₹12 lakh. Tax nil.

body.text: Lesson from Aman: under ₹12.75 lakh of salary, the old regime needs your taxable income to fall all the way to ₹5 lakh just to tie. Aman was ₹48,000 short, and the old regime's lack of marginal relief made those ₹48,000 cost him ₹22,984.

children.text: 2. Bhavna, ₹12 Lakh: Doing Everything Right, Still Losing

Bhavna, 29, is a UX researcher in Pune. Basic ₹4,80,000, HRA ₹1,92,000, rent ₹18,000 a month. She maxes 80C through EPF and an ELSS SIP, pays ₹20,000 for health insurance, and her employer deducts ₹2,500 of Maharashtra professional tax.
HRA exemption: least of ₹1,92,000, rent ₹2,16,000 minus ₹48,000 (₹1,68,000), and 40% of basic (₹1,92,000). Exemption ₹1,68,000.
New regime: ₹12,00,000 minus ₹75,000 is ₹11,25,000, below ₹12 lakh. Tax nil.

body.title: The Safe Zone
body.textWithBlank: For a salaried resident with no other income, the new regime is always at least as good as the old regime up to a salary of ₹___ lakh.
body.explanation: Up to ₹12.75 lakh of salary, new regime taxable income stays within ₹12 lakh and tax is nil. The old regime can at best match that, never beat it.

children.text: 3. Chirag, ₹14 Lakh: The Homeowner in the Sweet Spot

Chirag, 34, is an operations manager at a Delhi e-commerce company. He lives in his own flat in Dwarka, paying ₹2,00,000 of home loan interest a year. His EPF and loan principal fill 80C, he puts ₹50,000 into NPS, and pays ₹75,000 of health insurance for his family and his senior-citizen parents. This year he took his family to Srinagar and claims ₹60,000 of LTA. Delhi levies no professional tax.

body.title: Chirag: Travel Year vs Non-Travel Year

children.text: Old regime with LTA: ₹14,00,000 minus ₹50,000 minus ₹5,35,000 is ₹8,15,000. Tax is ₹12,500 plus 20% of ₹3,15,000 (₹63,000), total ₹75,500. Cess ₹3,020. Total ₹78,520. Without LTA, taxable income is ₹8,75,000, tax ₹12,500 plus ₹75,000, total ₹87,500, plus ₹3,500 cess, which is ₹91,000.

New regime: ₹14,00,000 minus ₹75,000 is ₹13,25,000. Slab tax is ₹60,000 plus 15% of ₹1,25,000 (₹18,750), total ₹78,750. Marginal relief does not apply because the ₹1,25,000 excess over ₹12 lakh is larger than ₹78,750. Cess ₹3,150. Total ₹81,900.

body.title: Why Did Chirag's Answer Flip?
body.question: Chirag's salary and investments are identical in both years. What single change moved him from the old regime to the new regime?
options: His home loan interest went above the ₹2 lakh cap
He did not claim LTA, so his benefits fell ₹60,000 and dropped below his ₹5,18,750 breakeven
The new regime's rebate started applying to his income
His parents turned 80, reducing his 80D limit
body.explanation: With LTA his benefits of ₹5,35,000 were above breakeven. Without it, ₹4,75,000 falls below breakeven. A salaried taxpayer with no business income can pick a different regime each year while filing, so Chirag can choose old in travel years and new in others.

children.text: 4. Esha, ₹22 Lakh: A Big Rent That Still Isn't Enough

Esha, 36, is an engineering manager at a Chennai SaaS company. Basic ₹8,80,000, HRA ₹4,40,000, rent ₹40,000 a month in Adyar. She maxes 80C, pays ₹25,000 for health insurance, and has ₹2,500 of professional tax. No home loan, no NPS, no LTA this year.

HRA exemption: least of ₹4,40,000, rent ₹4,80,000 minus ₹88,000 (₹3,92,000), and 50% of basic for Chennai (₹4,40,000). Exemption ₹3,92,000. Total benefits: ₹3,92,000 plus ₹1,50,000, ₹25,000 and ₹2,500, which is ₹5,69,500.

body.title: Esha Moves to a Bigger Flat
body.prompt: Esha moves to a ₹55,000 a month flat in Besant Nagar. Her basic salary and HRA stay the same. What is her new annual HRA exemption?
body.explanation: Rent minus 10% of basic is ₹6,60,000 minus ₹88,000, which is ₹5,72,000. But HRA received is ₹4,40,000 and 50% of basic is also ₹4,40,000, so the exemption is capped at ₹4,40,000. Her total benefits rise to ₹6,17,500, still below the ₹7,54,167 breakeven, so the new regime still wins even after paying ₹1,80,000 more rent a year.

children.text: 5. Gaurav, ₹40 Lakh: Where the Old Regime Earns Its Keep

Gaurav, 42, is a director at a Mumbai investment bank. Basic ₹16,00,000, HRA ₹8,00,000, rent ₹75,000 a month in Powai. He maxes 80C and 80CCD(1B), pays ₹75,000 of health insurance for his family and senior-citizen parents, and has ₹2,500 of professional tax.
Shortcut check: benefits exceed the ₹8 lakh breakeven by ₹2,17,500. At 30% plus cess, ₹2,17,500 × 0.312 = ₹67,860, exactly the difference.

body.text: Gaurav's win rests almost entirely on a ₹9 lakh rent. If he buys a home in Powai and stops paying rent, his HRA exemption disappears, and even with ₹2 lakh of home loan interest his benefits fall to about ₹4.78 lakh, far below ₹8 lakh. A single life event can reverse the decision, so treat the regime choice as a yearly review, not a one-time setting.

body.title: How the Answer Typically Shifts Across a Career

events.title: New regime, almost always
events.description: Salary is usually below ₹12.75 lakh, so new regime tax is nil and the old regime can only tie. Aman's profile.

events.title: Still new, even with discipline
events.description: Maxing 80C and paying moderate rent rarely clears the bar. Bhavna and Esha's profiles.

events.title: The swing zone
events.description: Breakeven is at its lowest. A home loan plus maxed deductions can win in some years and lose in others. Chirag's profile.

events.date: Senior role in a metro, renting
events.title: Old regime can win
events.description: A large HRA exemption on top of maxed deductions can clear ₹8 lakh. Gaurav's profile.

events.date: Buying a home or stopping rent
events.title: Recheck immediately
events.description: Losing HRA usually sends a high earner back to the new regime.

body.title: Jatin's Father Insists on the Old Regime
body.scenario: Jatin, 27, joins a Hyderabad pharma company on ₹9,50,000. He lives with his parents, so no rent. His EPF is ₹43,200 and he has a ₹15,000 health policy. His father, a retired bank manager who filed under the old regime for 35 years, insists that 'the old regime is always better for salaried people because of 80C' and tells him to buy a ₹1 lakh ELSS and declare the old regime.
body.prompt: Should Jatin follow his father's advice?
body.modelAnswer: No. In the new regime his taxable income is ₹9,50,000 minus ₹75,000, which is ₹8,75,000. That is below ₹12 lakh, so his tax is nil. In the old regime, even with the extra ₹1 lakh ELSS, his benefits would be ₹1,43,200 of 80C plus ₹15,000 of 80D, plus Telangana professional tax of ₹2,400, which is ₹1,60,600. His breakeven at ₹9.5 lakh is ₹4,00,000, just to reach nil tax. He would still pay tax in the old regime, so it cannot help. His father's advice was right for most of his own career, before the new regime's rebate existed. Jatin can still invest in ELSS if he wants equity exposure, but not for tax reasons.

body.title: Match Yourself to a Profile
steps: Note your gross salary and which of the five taxpayers is closest
Total your old regime benefits beyond the standard deduction, including HRA and any LTA claim this year
Look up your breakeven in the previous lesson's table
Compare, and if you are within about ₹50,000 of breakeven, run the full seven-step method
Set a reminder to recheck when you change homes, get a large raise or take a home loan

points: Up to ₹12.75 lakh of salary, the new regime wins or ties for every salaried resident, however disciplined their investing.
Maxing 80C and paying moderate rent is usually not enough to beat the new regime at mid-level salaries.
Homeowners near ₹13 to ₹15 lakh sit in the swing zone, where a single LTA claim can flip the result.
High earners paying large metro rents are the group most likely to benefit from the old regime.
Comparing total benefits against breakeven predicts the winner before any slab calculation.
Life events like buying a home, changing cities or a big raise can reverse the answer, so review it every year.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not tax advice. All taxpayers are illustrative, and figures reflect the rules applicable to tax year 2026-27 as understood at the time of writing, for residents under 60 without surcharge or special-rate income. Consult a qualified tax professional before filing.
